body:
What energy efficiency means

Energy efficiency means delivering a specified useful service or output with less energy input, or obtaining more useful output from the same energy input.

The useful service may be illumination, cooling, heating, water pumping, transport or industrial production. An efficient appliance or process reduces the energy required to deliver a comparable result.

For example, an energy-efficient lamp may provide approximately the same illumination as an older lamp while consuming less electricity. An efficient pump may lift the same volume of water through the same height using less energy.

Efficiency and conservation are related but different

Energy conservation broadly refers to reducing avoidable energy use. It can include improving efficiency and changing behaviour. Turning off unnecessary lights reduces energy consumption by eliminating an unneeded service. Replacing a lamp with a more efficient model reduces consumption while maintaining useful illumination.

ApproachMain changeExample
Energy efficiencyLess energy for comparable useful output.An efficient motor delivers similar mechanical output with lower energy input.
Energy conservationUnnecessary energy use is reduced or avoided.Switching off lighting in an unoccupied room.
Demand responseElectricity demand changes in response to time, price or an operational signal.Moving water pumping away from a high-demand period.
Renewable generationThe source of supplied energy changes.Using electricity generated from sunlight.

Installing solar panels changes the source of electricity; by itself, it does not necessarily make an inefficient appliance more efficient. Similarly, changing when electricity is used is not automatically the same as reducing the total energy used.

How efficiency is measured

For many devices, efficiency can be expressed as a comparison of useful output energy with input energy. Because real energy-conversion processes have losses, useful output is normally less than input energy.

In practical applications, a performance measure must match the service being delivered. A refrigerator may be compared by energy use under standard test conditions for a specified capacity; an air conditioner may be compared using a recognised seasonal performance measure; and an industrial plant may be assessed by energy consumed per unit of product.

Specific energy consumption (SEC) is energy consumed per unit of output, such as energy per tonne of material produced. A lower SEC generally indicates better energy performance when the processes, product quality, boundaries and other relevant conditions are comparable.

Energy intensity is not always a direct efficiency measure

Energy intensity expresses energy use relative to a broader activity measure, such as energy consumed per unit of economic output. An economy's energy intensity may fall because equipment becomes more efficient, but it may also fall because economic activity shifts from energy-intensive manufacturing toward services.

Therefore, falling energy intensity and improving technical energy efficiency are related but not identical observations.

Demand-side management

Demand-side management (DSM) refers to measures that influence the amount or timing of energy demand. It may include efficient appliances, improved building performance, agricultural pump efficiency, time-of-use tariffs and demand-response programmes.

Demand-side measures can reduce electricity consumption, moderate peak demand or both. Reducing peak demand can lower stress on generators and networks even when daily electricity consumption changes little.

Prelims focus

  • Energy efficiency concerns useful output relative to energy input.
  • Energy conservation can include switching off unnecessary energy use.
  • Specific energy consumption measures energy used per unit of output.
  • Energy intensity can change because of structural economic changes as well as efficiency improvements.
  • Demand-side management covers both energy-saving and demand-shifting measures.
  • Trap: A renewable energy source does not automatically make the appliance using its electricity energy-efficient.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Work and Energy, Chapter 11; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Infrastructure, Chapter 8; United States Department of Energy, Energy Efficiency vs. Energy Intensity, conceptual definitions; Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Standards and Labelling, objective and end-use energy reduction, updated 29 September 2026, consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Why buildings consume electricity

Buildings use electricity for lighting, fans, cooling, ventilation, water pumping, lifts, appliances and electronic equipment. In a hot climate, the amount of heat entering a building can strongly influence its need for mechanical cooling.

Energy efficiency begins with reducing unnecessary demand. Shading windows, limiting unwanted heat gain through roofs and walls, using suitable ventilation and daylight, and selecting efficient cooling equipment can reduce the electricity required to maintain acceptable indoor conditions.

Passive design and efficient equipment

Passive measures improve building performance through design rather than continuous mechanical operation. Appropriate orientation, external shading, insulation and natural ventilation are examples. Their effectiveness depends on climate, building use and local conditions.

Active measures include efficient air conditioners, fans, lighting, pumps, controls and other equipment. Automatic lighting controls can prevent unnecessary operation, while suitable temperature settings and equipment maintenance can improve practical performance.

Why efficient lighting saves energy

Incandescent lamps produce light by heating a filament, and a large part of their electrical input becomes heat rather than useful visible light. Light-emitting diode (LED) lamps generally provide similar illumination with substantially lower electricity consumption.

Illustrative lighting comparison

Suppose a 60 W incandescent lamp and a 10 W LED lamp provide approximately comparable light in a particular application. If each operates for 5 hours, the incandescent lamp consumes 0.30 kWh while the LED consumes 0.05 kWh.

The difference is 0.25 kWh for that day. Actual savings depend on the selected lamps, their light output and their hours of use; the wattages here are illustrative.

BEE star labels and appliance comparison

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) was established under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. Its Standards and Labelling programme, introduced in 2006, helps consumers compare the energy performance of specified appliances and equipment.

BEE uses a scale from 1 star to 5 stars, with higher stars indicating better energy efficiency under the relevant product criteria. Some appliance categories are subject to mandatory labelling, while others are covered voluntarily. The applicable rating schedules and covered products can change over time.

Star ratings should be compared within the relevant appliance category, capacity and rating period. A larger 5-star appliance may still consume more total electricity than a much smaller appliance because it provides a greater service or capacity. When available, the estimated annual energy-consumption figure is also useful.

A BEE energy star label communicates rated energy performance. A Bureau of Indian Standards conformity mark addresses compliance with applicable product standards. They serve different purposes; neither should be mistaken for the other.

Energy-efficiency building codes

The Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) 2017 established energy-efficiency requirements for qualifying commercial buildings. BEE's Energy Conservation and Sustainable Building Code (ECSBC) 2024 extends the building-performance framework to additional sustainability considerations.

The published ECSBC 2024 scope covers commercial or office buildings with a connected load of at least 100 kW or a contract demand of at least 120 kVA. Residential buildings are excluded from that code's specified scope. The legal application and enforcement of building-code provisions depend on the applicable government notification, adoption and local regulatory framework.

Eco Niwas Samhita (ENS) 2018 addresses residential building-envelope energy performance, including unwanted heat gain, heat loss, natural ventilation and daylight. It must not be confused with the commercial-building code.

Energy Performance Index

A building's Energy Performance Index (EPI) expresses energy consumption relative to floor area, commonly in kWh per square metre per year. Comparing EPI values requires attention to building type, operating hours, climate and other relevant conditions.

Prelims focus

  • BEE was established under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001.
  • The BEE Standards and Labelling programme began in 2006.
  • Within an applicable rating category, 5 stars indicate greater energy efficiency than 1 star.
  • ECBC 2017 and ECSBC 2024 concern energy-efficient commercial-building performance.
  • ECSBC 2024 specifies 100 kW connected load or 120 kVA contract demand as alternative scope thresholds for commercial or office buildings.
  • ENS 2018 concerns residential building-envelope performance.
  • Trap: A building or appliance's star rating should not be interpreted without considering the relevant category, capacity and rating criteria.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Electric Current and Its Effects, printed pp. 164–166, discussion of incandescent lamps, CFLs and LEDs; Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Standards and Labelling, updated 29 September 2026; BEE, Buildings Background, updated 30 April 2026, sections on ECBC 2017 and Eco Niwas Samhita 2018; BEE, Energy Conservation and Sustainable Building Code 2024, Chapter 2, Scope, consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Why energy efficiency matters in industry

Industries use electricity and other energy forms to run motors, pumps, compressors, fans, heating equipment and production processes. An improvement may save relatively little energy in one minute but produce substantial savings when equipment operates for many hours.

Industrial energy performance is best assessed against the quantity and quality of output. Producing more goods generally requires more total energy, but the energy consumed per unit of product may fall if production becomes more efficient.

Common industrial efficiency measures

  • Electric motors: efficient motors reduce electrical losses while supplying mechanical power.
  • Variable-frequency drives: where technically appropriate, motor-speed control can reduce unnecessary power use in variable-flow applications such as pumps and fans.
  • Compressed-air systems: repairing leaks and avoiding unnecessarily high pressure reduce wasted compressor energy.
  • Process heating: insulation and suitable waste-heat recovery reduce avoidable heat losses.
  • Maintenance: correctly maintained equipment can avoid energy waste caused by faults, friction, poor adjustment or deterioration.

Not every technology saves the same percentage of energy in every application. Savings depend on operating hours, load conditions, process requirements and the original equipment's performance.

Energy audits: finding and verifying opportunities

An energy audit is a systematic examination of how energy enters, moves through and is used in a facility. It seeks to identify consumption patterns, losses and opportunities for improved performance.

A useful audit process includes:

  1. Define the facility or process boundary and collect relevant energy-use information.
  2. Measure or estimate energy consumption by important equipment and activities.
  3. Establish a meaningful baseline that accounts for production or operating conditions.
  4. Identify and evaluate feasible efficiency improvements.
  5. Implement selected measures and compare subsequent performance with the baseline.

An audit identifies opportunities; it does not automatically save energy. Verified savings occur only when suitable improvements are implemented and perform as expected.

Perform, Achieve and Trade

The Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) mechanism, administered within India's energy-efficiency framework, is designed to improve Specific Energy Consumption (SEC) in identified energy-intensive establishments called Designated Consumers.

Under the PAT framework, a designated consumer receives an applicable SEC-reduction target. Performance is measured and verified against the prescribed baseline and target conditions. Eligible verified savings beyond the prescribed target can result in Energy Savings Certificates (ESCerts), which can be sold to designated consumers that need them to meet a shortfall against their targets.

ESCerts represent qualifying energy-efficiency performance under the mechanism. They are not the same as units of electricity sold on a power exchange, renewable energy certificates or carbon credits.

Agricultural pumping

Agricultural irrigation commonly requires electricity to operate water pumps. Efficiency measures include selecting suitable pumps, reducing avoidable water-flow restrictions, maintaining equipment and using efficient irrigation practices.

A pump should be assessed by the useful water-delivery service it provides, not merely by a lower electricity reading. Pumping less water can reduce consumption, but if crops require the same irrigation service, energy efficiency concerns delivering that service with less energy.

BEE's Agricultural Demand Side Management (AgDSM) programme addresses opportunities to improve the energy performance of agricultural pumping.

Municipal services

Municipal bodies use electricity for street lighting, drinking-water pumping, wastewater services and public buildings. Replacing inefficient streetlights with LEDs, maintaining pumps and using appropriate operating controls can reduce municipal energy consumption.

Municipal water systems may also manage the timing of pumping where storage and service requirements permit, helping reduce demand during stressed grid periods.

Prelims focus

  • Specific energy consumption is energy used per unit of production or other defined output.
  • An energy audit identifies opportunities and establishes a basis for evaluating savings.
  • Variable-frequency drives can improve efficiency in suitable variable-speed motor applications.
  • PAT stands for Perform, Achieve and Trade.
  • ESCerts relate to verified energy savings under PAT, not direct sale of electricity.
  • AgDSM concerns agricultural energy use, particularly pumping efficiency.
  • Trap: Installing an efficient pump does not establish actual savings unless operating conditions and delivered pumping service are considered.

[Sources: Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Perform, Achieve and Trade, objective, SEC targets, verification and ESCerts, updated 1 October 2026; BEE, Agricultural Demand Side Management Programme; BEE, Municipal Demand Side Management Programme; BEE, Energy Conservation Act framework and designated-consumer provisions, consulted 16 November 2026.]
